result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.k_shortest_paths()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find k shortest paths between source and target using Yen's algorithm. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L22645-L22761){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.k_shortest_paths( source, target, k, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![k shortest paths](/assets/graphs/k-shortest-paths.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A directed weighted graph with three routes from A to F. With k = 2, Yen's algorithm returns the cheapest path A, B, C, F (cost 4) in the accent color and the runner-up A, E, F (cost 5) in teal; the third route, through D (cost 6), stays faint." width="100%"} Finds multiple alternative paths ranked by total path weight/length. Useful for finding backup routes, route diversity analysis, or identifying critical edges. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Source node (integer ID or string label). [target]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Target node (integer ID or string label). [k]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of shortest paths to find. If fewer than `k` paths exist, returns all available paths. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[tuple[list[int], float]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of `(path, distance)` tuples sorted by distance (shortest first). Each path is a list of node IDs from source to target (inclusive). Returns empty list if no path exists or `k=0`. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Yen's algorithm (1971) finds the $k$ shortest simple paths by repeatedly running Dijkstra on modified graphs. Once the shortest path is known, each of its edges is temporarily removed in turn to generate candidate deviations; the next shortest path is whichever candidate has the smallest total weight, and the process continues until $k$ paths are produced or no more valid deviations exist. Total cost is $O(k \cdot n(m + n \log n))$, which is far more efficient than enumerating every simple path when $k$ is much smaller than the true count. All returned paths are simple (no repeated nodes). Yen's algorithm assumes non-negative edge weights, so on graphs with negative edges reach for `bellman_ford_shortest_path()` and prune manually. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Find alternative routes: ::: {#b9cba06e .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(weighted=True) .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_node(label="C") .add_node(label="D") .add_edge(source="A", target="B", weight=1.0) .add_edge(source="B", target="D", weight=1.0) # Route 1: A->B->D (cost 2.0) .add_edge(source="A", target="C", weight=1.5) .add_edge(source="C", target="D", weight=1.0) # Route 2: A->C->D (cost 2.5) .add_edge(source="A", target="D", weight=4.0) # Route 3: A->D (cost 4.0) ) paths = graph.k_shortest_paths("A", "D", k=3) [ ([graph.get_node(nid).label for nid in path], distance) for path, distance in paths ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [(['A', 'B', 'D'], 2.0), (['A', 'C', 'D'], 2.5), (['A', 'D'], 4.0)] ``` ::: ::: Unweighted graph (counts hops): ::: {#942314b4 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_grid_2d(rows=3, cols=3) # Grid: # 1 - 2 - 3 # | | | # 4 - 5 - 6 # | | | # 7 - 8 - 9 paths = graph.k_shortest_paths(1, 9, k=5) len(paths) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 5 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#f06e9929 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} paths[0][1] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 4.0 ``` ::: ::: Comparing the top two alternatives reveals how much longer the backup route is -- useful for identifying when a single edge is a critical bottleneck: ::: {#b5d1789e .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(weighted=True) .add_node(label="start") .add_node(label="mid") .add_node(label="end") .add_edge(source="start", target="mid", weight=1.0) .add_edge(source="mid", target="end", weight=1.0) ) paths = graph.k_shortest_paths("start", "end", k=2) len(paths) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` 1 ``` ::: ::: Since only one path exists in this graph, there's no backup route at all -- "mid" is a single point of failure between "start" and "end".
